newsitem.title: USA: U.S. agency says Mitsubishi interfering in sex case.
newsitem.headline: U.S. agency says Mitsubishi interfering in sex case.

text.p: The U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission said Wednesday that Mitsubishi Motors Manufacturing of America was interfering with potential claimants in the government's huge sex discrimination lawsuit.
"We object to the script that Mitsubishi is using to question women at the plant who have alleged they were victims of sexual discrimination," EEOC attorney John Hendrickson said.

In a filing made to the U.S. District Court in Peoria, Ill., which is hearing the case, the government accused Mitsubishi of improperly questioning female workers at its Normal, Ill., plant about past instances of sex discrimination.
The company, a unit of Japan's Mitsubishi Motors Corp., can only investigate current cases of alleged discrimination.

The government filing said Mitsubishi also asked women workers whether they planned on joining the EEOC's class-action suit, whether they took notes about what happened at the plant and asked for copies of the notes, and misinformed the women that they could qualify for damage awards even if they did not participate in the suit.
"We want to tell the women if they want to go anywhere with the case, do not talk to Mitsubishi about it," Hendrickson said.

The suit, announced by the EEOC on April 9, 1996, could seek up to $300,000 in damages for each of 700 employees at the plant, making it potentially the largest government sex discrimination suit ever brought.
It charged women workers at the sprawling plant were habitually groped, touched and harassed and that Mitsubishi managers did nothing about it.

A Mitsubishi spokesman would not comment on the latest filings, which are part of a battle over whether the government can send a mass mailing to women at the plant informing them about the pending lawsuit. Mitsubishi has objected to the mailing.

Mitsubishi executives have suggested they were hoping to settle the case and have made elaborate efforts to ameliorate any types of discrimination at the plant. But no settlement offers have been made, Hendrickson said.
He said an actual trial of the case was more than a year away.
